From a purely technical standpoint, bandwidth and computational resources (processing and storage space) are the problems. YouTube takes up a relatively large percentage of the Internet's total used bandwidth. It managed to get, IIRC, some extremely good deals on massive amounts of bandwidth early on, and after Google got it, that bandwidth could be paid for by them so long as they saw an advantage to continuing to operate the site, even without direct profit. At the moment, I don't see that changing in the near future. I hope I'm wrong, though.

Other posts that cite legal problems and other factors are also correct - especially if a lot of the laws depend on being able to use AI to efficiently scan for content that causes you problems, which is an extremely non-trivial project to undertake - but those are of academic interest if the site can't even get off the ground to simply exist as something more than someone's network hard drive attached to the Internet with a HTML5 video player front end.

Unfortunately I am not certain what, if anything, can be done to directly alleviate this at this time, except for possibly putting together a real company with very large amounts of capital.
